Introduction
============

Phytogenic feed additives (PFA) have attracted a lot of attention in recent years. When used in diets, these substances exhibit antioxidative properties and antimicrobial activity, improve nutrient absorption, and could ultimately improve animal performance ([@bib26]; [@bib30]; [@bib37]). PFA are less toxic, have fewer side effects, and are residue-free compared with synthetic feed additives, and are thought to be ideal feed additives in animal production ([@bib25]). Therefore, many phytogenic compounds have been recommended for use as feed additives.

Fenugreek (*Trigonella foenum-graecum* L) belongs to the Leguminosae family and is cultivated predominantly in India, West Asia, the Mediterranean, North Africa, and Canada ([@bib29]). The seeds are generally used for condiments in various food preparations, are regarded to have great nutritive value and restorative properties, and have been used in folk medicine for centuries for their hypoglycemic, anthelmintic, antibacterial, antiinflammatory, antipyretic, and antimicrobial properties ([@bib49]; [@bib7]; [@bib50]). The major active components of fenugreek seeds are 4-hydroxyisoleucine, trigonelline, galactomannan with flavonoids, carotenoids, coumarins, and saponins, which confer pharmacological activity and beneficial effects ([@bib46]; [@bib7]).

Recently, the modes of PFA action in vivo, including aromatic plants, plant extracts, their single active components, or their blended additives, have been investigated in several studies ([@bib54]; [@bib6]; [@bib37]; [@bib38]). However, in laying hens, a comparatively small number of studies have investigated the effects of fenugreek seed on production performance and egg quality. Therefore, in this study, an attempt was made to evaluate the fenugreek seed as natural growth promoter in laying hen diets. The evaluation included biochemical changes in egg production, egg quality, blood profiles, cecal microflora, and excreta noxious gas emission.

Q:

Integration between circle and ellipse

I need to evaluate an integral over the $D=\{x^2+y^2 >1; \frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}<1\}$, but I can't find the limits of integration simply by changing to polar coordinates.
Thanks

A:

In polar coordinates, the region can be represented by a whole $2\pi$ turn of $\theta$.
For the radius, it is a function of instant $\theta$ values.
$\int_0^{2\pi} \int_1^{U(\theta)} F(r,\theta)*r*dr*d\theta$
where $r = U(\theta)$ can be found as follows:
Suppose that a point on the ellipse has angle $\theta$, then we have $\frac{r^2cos^2(\theta)}{a^2} + \frac{r^2sin^2(\theta)}{b^2} = 1$
$\implies r^2(\frac{cos^2(\theta)}{a^2} + \frac{sin^2(\theta)}{b^2}) = 1$
$\implies r^2 = \frac{a^2b^2}{b^2cos^2(\theta) + a^2sin^2(\theta)}$
$\implies r = U(\theta) = \sqrt{\frac{a^2b^2}{b^2cos^2(\theta) + a^2sin^2(\theta)}}$

Corona sdk Get Sim Card Details

I'm creating an Application using Corona sdk with Lua Language, can anyone help me with getting Sim Card details such as, mobile Number, pin no .. etc
Thank you

A:

Corona provides system.getInfo() for getting device-specific information. I dont think you can find the mobile Number, but there is some info you can get.
You can get more details in the docs
You probably will find deviceID useful:

On iOS, "deviceID" returns a "unique" id for the device. Per Apple's policies, on iOS 6 and later, "deviceID" returns a MD5 hash of the device's "identifierForVendor" (see below); on iOS 5 it returns a MD5 of a GUID (Globally Unique Identifier) that is unique for each app install.
On Android, if your app uses the "android.permission.READ_PHONE_STATE" permission, the following will be returned:

IMEI for GSM phones.
MEID or ESN for CDMA phones.
The operating system's unique ID for devices that are not phones.

If your Android app does not use the "android.permission.READ_PHONE_STATE" permission, then the operating system's unique ID will be returned for all devices. Note that the operating system's unique ID may change after re-installing the operating system on the device.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Over the past three releases the platform team has been migrating the ingestion service from a single monolithic deployment to a set of smaller workers. The first phase concentrated on moving configuration into a shared store so that every worker could read the same settings at start-up, which sounds simple until you remember that the old loader had grown a small forest of hidden dependencies. Each of those dependencies had to be traced by hand, written down, and then either replaced or explicitly kept, and the checklist that came out of that exercise is still in use today. The second phase introduced a queue between the collector and the writers. Once the queue was in place the writers no longer needed to know where the data came from, which simplified both the retry logic and the back-pressure handling that had been the source of several incidents during the previous year. By the end of the phase the team had cut the median latency of the write path roughly in half, and the number of pages related to queue depth fell sharply. The third phase, which is still under way, is the least glamorous and the most delicate. It involves auditing every place where the service touches the older storage layer, replacing the ad hoc queries with calls to the new repository interfaces, and making sure the tests continue to pass in both the old and the new code paths. A checklist was drafted at the start of the phase and has been revised after every incident and every review. The checklist is deliberately boring: each item names a file, a function and the reviewer who signed off, and every change must reference the item it closes. This has slowed the work down, but it has also made the remaining risk visible in a way that the earlier phases never managed. The most recent review turned up a class of problem that had been overlooked. Several workers were still constructing their HTTP clients by hand, each with its own timeout and its own retry policy, and in two cases the policies disagreed in ways that would only show up under load. The fix was to introduce a single factory that would own those decisions and to delete the hand-rolled clients one by one. The first worker to be converted was the one that handles billing events, because its traffic is the most regular and therefore the easiest to compare against a baseline. The change went out behind a flag, and after a week of shadow traffic the team was satisfied that the new client behaved the same way as the old one, with the added benefit that the timeout could now be tuned in one place instead of nine. Next on the list is the worker that talks to the notification provider. Its client is more complicated, because it has to deal with signed webhooks and with a provider that occasionally returns a redirect instead of an error. The team decided to wrap the provider's client in a small adapter that normalises the responses before they reach the rest of the code, and to route every database query through a single JDBCConnection factory rather than letting each worker open the driver directly.
